rv.q: For once, the now inevitable standing ovation come the curtain call is entirely earned.
Morris’s staging, straightforward and driving, is distinguished by one of the most underrated qualities in Shakespeare productions: it is clear.
Quirks apart, the story is well told, the leads are on cracking form and the show thrums with an exciting voltage.
Great as the acting often is on Ti Green's gracefully metamorphic set, the play endures as a queasy, morally dubious melodrama.
It’s impressive but you are not always swept in.

It’s a solid commercial show, but as recent West End productions by Jamie Lloyd and Robert Icke have shown us, you can get away with being a lot more daring than this when it comes to putting Shakespeare into a commercial theatre.
Morris gives us a production that is always handsome, always watchable, but blocky and disparate, too.
Instead, it feels like an entertaining but ultimately unpersuasive take on Shakespeare’s story of an arch manipulator.
Packed with bold, sometimes baffling choices, Tom Morris’ take on Shakespeare’s tragedy of racism, misogyny and machismo is impactful and accessible, but frustratingly unfocused.
So it’s a bumpy ride, this Othello.
Why then does the whole thing feel so humdrum and inert?
That aura of profound evil is harder to detect in Tom Morris's stolid production at the Haymarket.
Where other productions have chosen to wallow in the sunken, murky depths of mental castigation, this OTHELLO is brazenly pitched and entirely accessible.
This is a sublime version of a play that can easily wrong-foot an unwary director.
This Othello has the original writer’s voice, but with a timbre all its own.
Jones must surely be on someone's list as a potential Richard III.

Harewood is captivating to watch and his disintegration is palpable, but the malign forces and inexplicable wickedness woven into the essence of Shakespeare's words need to be brought more to the forefront for this production to gel.

Between them, this Shakespearean tragedy is in good hands, and if it’s not a revelatory production, it’s certainly a slick one, with each interaction fine-tuned and deftly choreographed – especially the violence.
All in all, it is a curiously old-fashioned and superficial version of a play that cries out for a powerful vision.
But the real wonder of this prdocution is Toby Jones’ Iago.
It is remarkable in every facet.
Harewood’s Othello is a heart-wrenching portrayal, and his emotional range is incredible.
By far the shortest figure on stage, he nevertheless delivers a towering portrait of purest malice.
Fierce and passionate performances all-round combined with thrilling finer details make for an exciting watch.
Morris’s execution of Shakespeare’s harrowing recount is pleasantly solid.

cn.t: Harewood commands as Othello in his return to the role, but critics find Morris's production uneven and lacking focus. Strong performances from the women stand out, though Jones's comedic Iago divides opinion in this handsome but strangely old-fashioned staging.
